VERDICT: We've stumbled onto a hidden gem guys! It has everything an turn-based game should have, minus the cons I threw in, which can easily be overlooked from how in-depth the attack moves each character has, some battle scenes are pretty darn long, having a checkpoint helps but even with the help of that, can still feel long. title: Katana ZERO
analysis_text: I have to admit that I bought this game solely because of the positive reviews, which was a mistake I learned afterward. In my opinion, Katana Zero is nothing more than a basic platformer with an simple and generic gameplay. It isn’t even difficult enough to offer a real challenge. If you have ever played a 2D combat platformer before (even if it was just an old Flash game) you won't find anything new here. As for the story, although it features one interesting plot twist for a video game, the writing feels like it was done by a 12-year-old who watched too many R-rated movies. I won't tell any spoilers but what can I say is that it mixes random elements together into a narrative that becomes overly complicated just for the sake of it, before ultimately falling back on cheap, unoriginal clichés just to escape its own messy plot. Yeah, nice try, but that is not good storytelling. The soundtrack is also completely forgettable for me personally, except perhaps for the one track during the ending. But even this track fails to support either the characters' emotions or what is actually happening during the gameplay. All in all, Katana Zero has nothing truly special that makes it stand out from other 2D platformers. If you are fine with that, you might have some fun and perhaps even be impressed by the single plot twist I mentioned. However, anyone else who, like me, was looking for something truly great will be disappointed. I cannot recommend it.

title: Katana ZERO
analysis_text: This game straight up sucks and its style is straight up plagiarized from Hotline Miami which is a better game in every single way. Again, this game is garbage. The writing sucks, the combat sucks, and the level design sucks. The game is mechanically very easy and manufactures "difficulty" through trial and error one hit kill nonsense. It is almost more like a puzzle game than an action game. Additionally, the stealth sections are some of the worst designed gameplay I've ever experienced, on par with 15 minute long Flash games from the early 2000s. Overall, it's just awful, awful gameplay. Also, the music is exceedingly mediocre and everyone who praises it is just exposing themselves as rubes who only listen to generic pop music. Go listen to some real Electronica and then come back to this slop to realize just how derivative and simple it is. The game is 3 hours long with half of that being painfully paced, dreadfully pretentious, low quality slop writing that seems like it was written by a middle schooler and retails for $15. That would be a massive ripoff even if the game was good. The way the story sections are paced make it obvious that the dev knew the game was far too short and did what ever he could to pad out the run time. This game should be priced at $3 MSRP. With several million in sales and a whopping 98% "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating on Steam, this game is in the running for most overrated game of all time. Rating - 2/10

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: Small Saga was pretty mediocre. There are some pretty cute moments where I enjoyed the characters and how they reacted to the events unfolding. However, the overall story operates at so much of a breakneck pace that it makes character development incredibly jarring; characters will flip motivation on a dime just to railroad the main plot. In the span of ~6 hours, you [spoiler] help a child run away from home, start a prison break which leads to overthrowing an authoritarian town and installing a new leader, start a revolution against the monarchy, overthrow a slaver, and help a person reconcile their past[/spoiler]. The game honestly tries to do too much too fast, which makes transitioning between main story beats turbulent. This results in characters not realistically offering pushback on others or having instantaneous changes of heart. Simultaneously, new ideas and information on people’s past are constantly introduced, but never meaningfully utilized or elaborated on. Many of the main story conflicts are resolved off screen and are only barely mentioned being resolved in a few sentences. A few characters are particularly loathsome with cringy dialogue in the form of forced memes. There are also several references to memes that were topical at the time. Constant attempts at humor are made but they mostly fall flat. The story takes up the vast majority of the game with some light amount of boss combat near the climax of each plot point. The combat is extremely vapid to the point it feels like a fantasy story masquerading as an RPG. There aren’t any meaningful decisions to make in terms of building character skills or gear. In fact, the game has several skills that increase damage to different types of enemies that either appear in only 2 combats or only in one chapter. I never felt in danger during combat and it boiled down to spamming damage abilities with no thought. It is very dissonant to be a meek rodent trying to rise up against larger creatures while combat is never dangerous. The final boss of the game was doing attacks that did 2 damage to me. There is a lack of polish that hampers the storytelling experience. Many important story moments had no music or ambient sound that made reading the dialogue emotionally hollow. Nearly every cutscene in the game used fades to black to hide actions being performed, items being placed, etc. There are also many incredibly long walkways between story areas that don’t serve any purpose to gameplay or storytelling. They don’t build atmosphere and just pad playtime as you meander through empty halls in dead silence. Overall, I found Small Saga to be entertaining enough to want to see the game through. The game was gifted to me and I think if I had spent the $15 myself, I would be more disappointed. For that reason, I can’t really recommend this game to others for its price. The plot is too hasty and needs to take more time so that many of the introduced threads are not hand waved away.

analysis_text: Months of pure dopamine. Vampire Survivors is one of those games that somehow manages to be incredibly simple and ridiculously engaging at the same time. It’s fun, challenging, chaotic, and gives you that huge dopamine hit when everything comes together. Sometimes I played it while waiting for the bus. Sometimes I just had a 15-minute session when I needed a break. Other times I could disappear into it for hours, hunting for new weapons, upgrades, evolutions, and everything else the game throws at you. And the chaos on screen is genuinely beautiful. Watching the screen turn into an absolute storm of enemies, projectiles, effects, and damage numbers while your build keeps getting stronger never really gets old. I spent months with this game, and when that final achievement finally popped, I was honestly sad. I wasn't ready for it to be over. Now I'm just waiting for more content and another DLC, because I absolutely want an excuse to jump back in. And the fact that this incredible game came from one developer is honestly magical. What started as such a simple concept became one of the most satisfying games I've played. Highly recommended. I just wish I could experience that first playthrough again.

In the end, [spoiler]I chose Niko because I felt like there was literally no reason for me to choose the world that didn't make me try to care about it. [b]Given these points, I would recommend games like Undertale or OMORI to someone looking for a game with this kind of theme. title: OneShot
analysis_text: Let me be clear I don't think that this is a bad game. If there was a neutral option I would have picked it, I just have a little bit more negative than positive. First the positives. I like the character designs. Everyone really sticks out and the different kinds of creatures make the world feel unique. I think that the concept of not only having to solve puzzles that have a point and click adventure style, but also having to do things on your computer is a nice concept and it had a few puzzles that I thought were really cool and had a lot of fun playing with. Niko is a very cute and fun protagonist and I definitely grew to really like him over the time i spent playing the game. My problems though are as follows. I think that the character writing is overall weak other than Niko. We don't get enough time with each characters or have conversations enough about them to really get an idea of who they are, and it's really disappointing. you always feel like the characters are just in the world that you are passing through and you only ever interact with them because you need them to solve a puzzle. It's a dang shame, because I really like the designs of each of the characters, I just wish there was more substance there. I wish that there were more dialogue options when interacting with Niko to give you more of a relationship with him. As I said previously, I really like him as a character, but I wanted more things to talk to him about and maybe have him remember things you told him before and have reactions to things in the world based on that. You have a few moments like that around the end, but you don't get to really interact with him in depth more than the main plot demands, and even then you only get two options that don't cover a lot of ground. The Solstice route, which could have been upping the anti by a lot in some really interesting ways as well as fleshing out the characters more, ended up being the weakest part of the game. The puzzles were either things you have already seen or were things that were done in a way more impressive manner in earlier playthroughs, leading to an underwhelming feeling when doing them. The characters get a little bit more dialogue but end up just treading over the same ground that they already did in the fist route rather than adding to the characters in any meaningful ways. some of which don't even get names until the end of the game. Some of the new characters are okay, but ultimately they just take away time we could be connecting further with the already established characters just to add more characters that we spend even less time with. The overall tension in the story felt force and predictable, and the ending felt cheap like it made everything that happened before meaningless. it was very disappointing. Overall it is not a bad game and has real potential and cool game mechanics, it just feels like it always falls short of the mark and leaves me wanting more.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Ikenfell is one of literally thousands of 2D JRPG ripoffs infesting Steam, although at least this one was "genuinely" made instead of being asset flipped from the godawful RPG Maker construction kit. That doesn't mean, by a long shot, that this lazy, badly done console port is the kind of game any self respecting PC gamer would touch with a 10' pole. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard. A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result. There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings. There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. PC gamers will be insulted by the presence of console peasant children's toy controller prompts, despite this being on PC. Developers should try to be aware which platform they're developing for. Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies. Compromises were made to cater to the inferior console gaming appliances that the game was designed for. These are unfortunate compromises and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was a second thought for the console-centric developers. The game is deficient as a result of these choices, and would have been so much better without the handicaps that designing games for consoles forces upon a game. Once more, console peasants have made gaming worse for everyone. These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game. Ikenfell has a truly insulting price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games (with 3D graphics instead of pixelcrap!), let alone the sheer number of free games available on Steam. Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, and the questionable ethical nature of the developer and/or their associates (as outlined above), this is impossible to recommend.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Ikenfell has potential but squanders a lot of it through a lot of small issues that end up building into one massive frustration. The core gameplay of this game is similar to the Mario and Luigi RPG games from the Nintendo GBA and DS days. Its a turn based RPG that requires you to learn the impact point of moves so you can hit the action button at the right time to either muliply the damage you give or reduce damage taken. The system works competently enough in this game and isn't all that hard to get to grasp with. Even then there are accessibility options in the game that allow the player to automate these if they struggle with their reactions. In my opinion accessibility options are always worthy of praise. However battles feel like they take an age. Not that they are difficult or challenging but they all start to feel like they drag after a while. Maybe the designers were trying to go for the same sort of experience you get in the Persona games where even an encounter with even the simplest of enemies could expand into explosive clashes but it kind of just falls flat here. Unlike Persona this game lacks the masterful presentation those games have which make those long battles interesting to play and engaging to take part in. The snails pace of the battle also starts to bleed into other areas of the game after a while. The story is glacial at revealing further plot twists and developments. With no sub plots or side activities that support the main story I honestly started to physically feel the passing of time. Either the main plot needed more to happen, move at a much faster pace or be supplemented by other side stories to keep itself interesting. The final straw for myself came when I had to find several keys to enter a location. To do so you have to wander a small but very bland map in what I can only describe as a pixel hunt. Nothing is more infuriating than when I start to feel I am wasting time without fun in a video game. With that said I don't recommend Ikenfell but I do hope the developers do carry on with their work. I feel there is a good game almost ready to be made here and just falters in too many areas for it to be truly enjoyed. I'd like to imagine with some time they will be able to make more cohesive and engaging stories and gameplay.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: [b]Impostor Factory[/b] serves as the missing link that finally brings the SigCorp saga together. While initially presented as a standalone murder mystery, it slowly reveals itself as a deeply connected narrative that ties [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes into a single, coherent whole. What begins as an intriguing game gradually transforms into one of Kan Gao's most confident and emotionally resonant stories. Narratively, Impostor Factory feels like a return to form. The main theme is just as approachable as [i]Finding Paradise[/i] while having the same finesse in storytelling as [i]To the Moon[/i], taking the best of both worlds. The central twist was genuinely unpredictable to me, yet completely logical in hindsight, which is a very difficult balance to strike. The game also manages to expand [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] as a character: questions that lingered across previous entries are addressed, adding layers of depth that recontextualize his behavior throughout the series. Overall, Impostor Factory feels like the perfect conclusion to a theoretical trilogy. It respects the legacy of the previous games while standing on its own, delivering one of the strongest narrative experiences in the series. [h1]The Good[/h1] + Perfectly ties together [i]To the Moon[/i], [i]Finding Paradise[/i], and the minisodes + Adds significant depth to [spoiler]Neil[/spoiler] and answers long-standing questions about him + Feels like a natural and satisfying conclusion to the trilogy + Storytelling is top tier, easily the strongest aspect of the game + Soundtrack and ambience are once again flawless + Plot twist manages to be the central piece that ties everything together while still being surprising + Baited by Kan Gao by thinking this was just a "murder mystery thriller featuring multiple casualties", unrelated to the past games + Still using the greatest game engine of all time, RPG Maker, to its full potential + We can finally run!! [h1]The Bad[/h1] - None. Well played. (first game I review where I have zero complaints, quite an achievement!) [i]Is it wrong if all I really wanted to be is just another lavender?[/i] [h2]10 / 10 - IGN[/h2]

I really loved this puzzle RPG game. The storytelling starts off a bit cringy but gets better very soon into the game. You play as Maritta who is searching for her sister that didn't come home for the summer from Ikenfall, her magic school. Here you'll enter a world that is very unknown for Maritta, but the characters you meet will also feel on edge because there is something weird going on in the magic world. I love how every party member has their own story and characteristics, which plays a big part in the story. They are not generic party members at all. title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: After two emotionally moving masterclasses in video game storytelling from this developer — "To the Moon" and "Finding Paradise" — I really wanted to love this third installment, but I think they may have bit off somewhat more than they could chew here. Impostor Factory wants to be this much darker, more cerebral plot, with mysterious murders and time loops, and then it dovetails into a much more linear version of the sort of story we've come to expect from Freebird Games, chronicling one person's life from start to finish, and then it tries to tie everything together with a very meta plot twist. But this means the tone of the story is all over the place. Sort of an aside, but there's also a plot thread that really gets under my skin, and it hampered my enjoyment of this game. [spoiler]There is a point where the timeline diverges in response to an important family-planning decision. In the "bad" timeline, the mother's life is prioritized over her child's, the child lives a very short and tortured life, and this leads to the family splitting apart forever after he dies. In the "good" timeline, the child's life is prioritized over his mother's, and he grows up to do great things and the family stays together, but his mother must now live out the rest of her days battling a terminal illness that would've been cured otherwise. It smacks of those arguments that anti-abortion activists use: "no matter what you might be going through, or how much your own life might be put at risk from pregnancy, you should absolutely give birth because your child might theoretically become the next Einstein."[/spoiler] I really did not like this undertone to the story, for reasons I hope are obvious. Both of this developer's previous titles made me cry, or at least tear up a bit. Here, I mostly felt confused and annoyed by the end.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: I really enjoyed To The Moon and Finding Paradise. They could be a bit overly sentimental but ultimately the emotional themes resonated with me and I came away from them thinking they had something valuable to say. Sadly, the 3rd game in the series, Impostor Factory, falls flat on its face in this regard. This was my experience of the narrative of Impostor Factory: Act 1 - The game seems like it's doing something completely different from the first 2 games in the series. It's creepy and exciting and I was curious as to where it was going. Act 2 - The novel, creepy, exciting bits fall away and the game now proceeds with a boring, drawn-out rehash of many of the same exact themes and narrative beats of the first 2 games in the series. Act 3 - The game now throws some twists at you to reconcile Acts 1 and 2, fully cementing the fact that you have no real reason to care about anything that's happening. It attempts to manufacture some last minute stakes that ring utterly hollow. It is a truly misjudged narrative that feels gimmicky, boring, and annoying to progress through. Add to this the fact that the already limited gameplay of the series has been stripped down even further and I see little reason to recommend this game.

title: Impostor Factory
analysis_text: ....wait a sec, please.... *yourjaguarlover dabs his puffy eyes* ahem. I played the Freebird games in the wrong order. Or did I? In any case, I have now completed the series. It is a series I have a deep, deep love for and here's what I think (no spoilers, it would be a travesty to do so) Not for the first time, I (wrongly) assumed this would be an ancillary part of the series, a spin-off, a side-quest. In fact, it's the beginning, and the end and the middle and all of it. For *reasons* I am actually super glad I played this AFTER The Beach Episode because the way all the final pieces of this story clicked together truly blew my mind and left me so satisfied and ethereally happy, in the way that only understood tragedy can provide. If you aren't aware this, like all games in the series are basically visual novels with very minor interaction - but those interactions are crucial, critical to how the game delivers its timing, its drama and its heartfelt, sorrowful truth. I can't stand visual novels but Kan Gao delivers something I have never seen before or elsewhere, by making you not just a viewer but somehow an essential third party to it even though you do not appear in it. And in this instalment, more-so than ever, you are in these characters hearts and souls and stories - irrevocably linked somehow so you feel every single emotion and unfolded plot development (assuming you have at least played To The Moon and ideally some others) If you played games in this series, you'll know there will be sorrow, bittersweet tears and swooping joyous releases of emotion - this instalment delivers those in spades but also true horror, grief and awful awful tragedy as you feel part of decisions you wish you could take back. It's all a part of the journey that makes you feel so whole by the finale. I wax lyrical about these games, I know, and I also occasionally talk about video games story relevancy to art and literature. This series, right from the beginning of To The Moon is the ace card in that argument. I'd go as far as to say it's a genre in itself - a videogame only by rote of you using a screen and a keyboard to experience it, a movie that could never be made, a story so sprawling and intricate that could never be just written down in words. What seems like another RPG Maker, low visual fidelity follow-the-story is actually something that transcends other media for me in terms of experience. Even those pixel graphics contain so much nuance and detail, the sound - always just perfect and beautiful and intrinsic - those few key presses and mouse moves and clicks which are literally purposefully timed by a maestro. Ladies and gentlemen, these games ARE art. Kan Gao is a genius and a legend to me, I owe him so much as a person who plays all kinds of video games pretty much all of the time for bringing me something so different -unique even - and being the only person I have ever been happy to break my heart so many times and in so many ways. When we ask what makes a good videogame, the same is true as in any walk of life. Have a vision, work out whats needed to deliver that vision in exactly - the tiniest - detail you intended and never, ever compromise. There's nothing like these games and they are all 10/10 perfect creations to me. This one is a moving masterpiece that fits right in

title: To the Moon
analysis_text: To the Moon sits in a very distinct category as far as games go. It is focused on story and emotion. The game mechanics are not important; you are not being punished for doing anything wrong during a puzzle, so leave your competitive side at the door when you press play. The game takes some ideas from Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, but it still feels original. This comparison should give away the main concept of the game. If you loved the movie, I am sure you will also love this game. The music, composed by Kan Gao, also the creator of the game, is amazing. It fits the game perfectly; it never feels boring, even if you stay in the same scene for minutes. The songs have a calming, homey feel that never becomes annoying despite their repetition. The art matches the story; it always surprises me how pixel art can show a character's emotions so well. The colours remind me of autumn, and everything feels very atmospheric. It's a beautiful game to look at. I want to underline that, as with all different mediums of art, games can also have an emotional impact, and To the Moon will work your tear ducts to the maximum. Have some tissues ready, just in case.

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: [h2]A solid addition to the world of "To the moon"[/h2] I think if I had to pick, I'd probably say I preferred to the moon, but that could just as well be because I played it first, it's not uncommon to be biased towards your introductory game or episode of a series. I thought this was pretty sweet, it's still a narrative game with some puzzle elements, but the writing is great, if the writing wasn't as top tier as it is I definitely wouldn't have enjoyed this or to the moon one bit, and for a dyslexic person who struggles to maintain focus when reading, that says a lot to it's quality. The sprites are mostly just the same as to the moon, but still just as amazing, I did notice some weird mixels during Neil's transformation sequence, and some tiny spots where pixels didn't line up fully or were a bit jittery, nothing that'd ruin your experience but they did stick out to me during my playthrough. The music is phenomenal as you'd expect, maybe a bit samey at times, but better that than incohesive, a little more variety in some spots wouldn't hurt, and might heighten the impact of the emotional tracks when they come in, but again, nothing that'll detract from your experience. I played "A bird story" prior to this, and honestly I didn't quite get the connection, I mean, yeah, same character, it's a standalone look into a point of his life that's been abstracted, but for a chunk of the game I was just like "so she's the bird maybe?" But no, the bird is kind of just insignificant outside of "A bird story", which was kind of sad to me, but it is what it is, it's not like it ruined the experience for me. I think Asher could've done with a bit more character development maybe, more screentime, more moments with his family, but the story does go on a bit as is, so I'm not mad they didn't try to shove more in there; I [i]am[/i] mad about the walk speed though, it's just too slow, for "To the moon" I think it worked better because the environments were a bit smaller, sometimes you'd be on a long walk from one area to another, but having most segments be smaller walkable areas made the walk speed feel reasonable for the majority of it, here it felt like it was padding the length of the game a bit, a sprint button at least would've been appreciated, I'm not saying we need to be running the whole game, just a slight increase, because as is, I felt like the walkspeed alone added at least half an hour to my playtime, maybe even a whole hour. But overall, great game, I thought it was really sweet, teared up a little at the end, I had minimal gripes with the story, the art, the music, the gameplay, I'm not gonna pretend there wasn't any friction with any of it, but it's so minimal compared to the master craftsmanship behind the entire rest of the game that they're just insignificant. If you're not a narrative game type, or you prefer games with intricate gameplay mechanics, multiple routes or endings, maybe this won't be for you, but if you like a good story with some interactive elements, I think this is worth your time.

analysis_text: 9/10, subtracted 1 because I couldn't find paradise. (Kidding, of course. I really like the game.) The people who worked on this lovely little gem throw the concept of a genre around like a hot potato. That isn't a bad thing, mind you; I find it amusing and effective. One moment I'm laughing at Neil and Eva's usual banter, then the next I'm feeling uneasy because... well, I'm not here to spoil anything. But if you liked To the Moon and want to see what other funny and emotionally heavy shenanigans the scientists get up to, I recommend checking this game out. The little details such as characters' background actions, along with how expressive everyone is, seemed to improve a lot here. I loved the sprite work. It felt like the world I was watching was really alive. I thought the game wouldn't affect me as much as TtM did, so I really didn't expect to be so invested that I ignored all my plans for the day just to finish it. It packed a punch in more ways than one and made me rethink some aspects of my life. Just the music playing when I saw the title screen for the first time was enough to make me realize I was in for an interesting ride. I find it funny how the new client and his wife are also musically inclined, though. Are all musicians bound to have bittersweet lives? Should I be concerned...?

title: Finding Paradise
analysis_text: Finding Paradise is the sequel to the game that broke my heart, and while it didn't have that particle lightning-in-a-bottle effect on me, that is not because I think the game is worse. Part of the shock of To the Moon to me was how much I personally related to it, and that I was not expecting it to be so deeply emotional. I expected something similar from Finding Paradise, and on that it does succeed. This game does everything you would want from a sequel for To the Moon. It gives us another heartbreaking life to relive and expands on the formula. Whereas previously we went back in time, seeing a love story in reverse to try and figure out what the hell is going on in this guy's memories, we instead see a beginning and an ending that seem impossible to reconcile, with similarly heartbreaking reveals as we try and figure out what the hell is wrong with this guy's memories. It also manages to inject some real tension and more character moments for our Sigmund crew. Despite knowing how the memory gimmick works, finding paradise manages to keep the framing device fresh, and even expands on it from the first game. Play it anyway. It isn't quite as bittersweet as the first game, but it is still incredibly bittersweet. It hurts, it really does. If you liked the first one, play this one.

title: Long Gone Days
analysis_text: Really tempted to jokingly label it as "Metal Gear Undertale". This is an indie JRPG that combined a pretty grounded for a JRPG scifi plot involving modern war... and also a story about friendship. Generally it sticks very closely to this older JRPG canon of having parties, equipment giving stat boosts, taking turns using abilities or attacks or items, travelling trough locales and engaging in dialogue, all that. It's faithful to older 2D JRPGs to a fault, despite more modern art style it can be pretty slow with animations, transitions and prompts to perform actions. During certain dungeon crawls there's a lot of air vents to crawl and each gives confirmation prompt if you do want to do it where a single interact would have been enough. A lot could have been done smoother, really. New ideas are playing safe too, like ability to pick where to aim in JRPG combat, avoiding armor at chance of missing or reducing damage further to hit a painful weakspot and make enemy skip turns. It's interesting but under-utilized, and the limited hit spot variety is sad, could have had stuff like shooting specific equipment to disable specified abilities or induce greater variety of effects. Now, the story: a naive but principled rookie soldier, fully raised in a militarized society of The Core subterranean state deserts after discovering he's tasked to kill innocents, convincing another soldier to flee with him, on his way encountering other characters he teams up with to survive and then confront Core's ambitions. It's... not too sophisticated and you can see quite some twists before the characters do so to be fair everyone feels lowkey naive. But it kinda feels like an anime, young adult adventure sort, so it works thematically? Personally my favourite bits in this one were the towns you visit and roam relatively free in, full of things to discover, tiny quests and scenes spent with main characters. There's even an aspect where you need a specific language speaker to actually communicate with anyone else which doesn't have major impact beyond "can only meaningfully interact after X joins you" but it does add believeability to settlements. This is fine. I guess if you wanna play a JRPG but wanna go for more martial theme this will do well. It's nothing revolutionary though.

title: Vampire Survivors
analysis_text: The part of my brain that enjoys roguelikes has been fried from over-stimulation, leaving me feeling like I just played the closest thing that exists to a gambling-less slot machine. The power curve is very unsatisfying. Most runs take about ten minutes to ramp up, give you 3-4 minutes of feeling strong, and then fill the screen with so much crap you may as well be looking at a Jackson Pollock. For all of this, the gameplay is minimal. There's a point in pretty much every run where you no longer need to dodge and can just afk, and it happens earlier than it should. I also find there's very little run variety. Items for the most part do very similar things with the occasional dud and gamebreaker thrown in, and most characters play as carbon copies of one another that feel arbitrarily nerfed/buffed based on their starting stats and items. There are some unique gimmick characters like Babi Onna who only fires her weapons while moving, but these are maybe like 4 characters in a cast of dozens. As it is however, this straddles a very awkward space where it's too involved to be an afk/clicker type game, and too much of a brainless flashy colours number-go-up game to lean more into its roguelike, compendium unlocking elements. It's cheap and it'll flood you with enough sensory input that for a while you can forget that you're going to die one day. At a similar price point, I'd rather just drink a beer and watch TV instead.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: I think this game was amazing. The art is great, the story compelling (i couldn't stop playing it until i was finished even though I was in the middle of uni exams), the music got stuck in my head(although it tends to repeat...), but the thing that made me LOVE this game were the characters. Every dialogue felt real, the main cast all felt like fleshed out people who existed outside of the cutscenes, with their own problems and little worlds. They even all have different religions which I was compelled by. Siffirin's breakdown was so immersive and raw, partly because we both shared the frustration of having to go through the whole game over and over and over again (the battles felt tedious quickly but I just pushed through it, just as siffirin had to). The dynamics between the main cast were heartwarming and cozy and fleshed out the characters even more. It's one of the sweetest found families I've seen :] I think this game is underrated and you should play it!

analysis_text: a really unique and fun little RPG set in a world where animals are sentient and see humans as gods. you are Guts- I mean Verm, a mouse who lost his bother and his tail due to the yellow god (an exterminator), and swears vengeance upon them, promising to slay the very gods with his god forged greatsword, titan reaper (a pocket knife). title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: Playing this game was an experience I will never forget! :D The art and music draws you in, but the comradery between Isabeau, Odile, Mirabelle, Bonnie, and Siffrin as well as the twists and turns along the way keep you locked in. I had so much fun just reading the dialogue between characters. So much humor and charm behind nearly every interaction, even with the people in the town. Their friendship is an anchor in a world of chaos, and it's so wholesome despite the pressure they faced. I also liked how the battle system was based on rock. paper, scissors, even if it did make combat less complex as a turn-based game. My only gripe with the battle system was how tedious it became to battle over the course of the game. I eventually found an item that allowed me to circumvent some of the tediousness which was nice. My main complaint with the game is that there are certain parts that feel unnecessarily frustrating and difficult to complete. I would say Act 4 gave me the most trouble and I actually had to go through a walkthrough twice in order to finally pass it. The story, characters, art, and music make it worth it but it does feel a little too much at certain points even if I understand it relates to a core part of the story. I highly recommend this game! This is one of those games that can change your life by playing. I will never forget my buddies Siffrin, Odile, Isabeau, Mirabelle, and Bonnie ; u; <3

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: Gameplay wise, incorporating timing is used to make players get more involved with the combat system. How engaging it is varies from person to person, though the pitfall of "losing a match because you mistime a single action" ala Virgo vs the Zodiacs is not present, which should give you a glimpse of the overall difficulty. Personally, I recommend new players to turn on semi-auto for the first few chapters to get a sense of the timing without trivializing everything. Though be warned that once you master the rhythm part, most boss fights become cakewalks. The boss fights are also pitfalls of the game: Because of the 3xN nature of the grid, a single enemy will be severely restricted mobility wise, which, combined with traps, allow for the players to pummel bosses relentlessly. There is also no mana, so resource management isn't a concern. This means that bosses are difficult not because of their own patterns or gimmicks, but mostly because they throw a bunch of minions at you, sometimes to the point of blocking movement altogether, though I guess that's the point. Of course, at any time players can press the "I win" button, which I applaud for inclusivity - video games are for everyone after all. Speaking of inclusivity, the story absolutely does that theme justice. So as to not get into spoiler territories, I'll just say that you have representation of all sexual orientation and genders: from lesbians, gay, straight, to enbies and genderqueer... It shows a more realistic representation of life, that your identities matter, and most importantly, that people can accomplish great things regardless of background. Though I do wish that their identities factor into the plot or their character arc a bit more, but it's within the developers' imperative to create a fully tolerant world free of bigotry, and I respect that. [spoiler] My biggest peeve with the game is its epilogue, in which Gilda and Maritte are stated to have broken up because they love someone else, but Gilda is still shown to be completely head over heel for her ex. It's good that they remain amicable and avoid the stereotype of breaking up, but is it too much to ask for a happy ending for Gilda. She's my favourite character and now i just feel bad for her. The little gay disaster is really relatable and it's sad that after an entire game of bottling up her feelings she didn't get even a confession scene to end her arc with :(( [/spoiler] Edit: apparently you can buy the entire game's OST on bandcamp, so I retract that part of my review.

title: Long Gone Days
analysis_text: I went into this game very much hoping that I would like it. I won't lie, the visuals alone were enough to sell me on it but ultimately after reaching the end point of this version I can say that it had little bearing on the efficacy of the game. [ GAMEPLAY ] So, what went wrong? Let's start with the gameplay. The combat works like this: You can either hit the enemy with a % chance to miss, or you can hit the enemy guaranteed at a cost. Like, a cost that only has an unreliable way of being renewed. The simplicity of the skills really, really leaves a lot to be desired. Apart from the distinct lack of strategy in a turn based military RPG (use multi-hit attacks on multiple enemies and heal allies who are dying does not count), this feels like an awkward way to handle combat. It's a subtle pressure for you to not use your abilities as much as possible because you never know when the next morale (MP) boost will come since it's tied to major story events, but at the same time, the game is easy enough that you can just regular attack your way through the entire game save for a few instances those AoE attacks become relevant. Personally, I kept missing chest shots and pretty reliably hit head shots so it gave the impression that it didn't really matter that much which one I picked. If I'm going to miss anyway, might as well chance it on the higher damage option, which worked out pretty swimmingly. The slowness of the combat combined with being generally unstimulating leaves it feeling very much like an afterthought. Seems late in development to revamp the combat system, but if there's still room for hefty change I'd strongly recommend it because as it stands, the gameplay is a chore to sit through. The fact that I can't distinguish who can equip which armor whenever I pick up new gear is mildly annoying... [ WRITING ] For a game that tackles some serious subjects, it certainly doesn't feel like it takes itself very seriously. Okay, sure, maybe a missed opportunity but not a deal breaker. What does it have to offer instead? Well, not a whole lot. Because of its wishy-washy, half-serious tone, any kind of grim or otherwise dramatic scene that is presented is undercut by non-committal platitudes that lacks any weight or emotion. Rather than provoking feelings that are genuinely moving or rousing, we get these sort of... deflated anime speeches that feel like they don't have anything real to say. This could be salvageable if the game decided to lean more heavily into comedy or other more light-hearted avenues to make up for this, but it doesn't do that either. Instead, it sits in this awkward middle of the road space where it's NOT serious enough to be a properly gripping tale of injustice and revolution, but it's TOO serious to be a fun adventure about friendship and growth. I think it's possible to do both honestly, but the writing is much too timid to actually push for it. The actual dialogue feels quite stilted as well, falling short of giving players the impression that these are believable characters, or even that we should be invested in them. Their speech patterns are just barely distinct enough to not blend together, and it's all kind of robotic overall. This is not helped by the fact that the personalities of these characters suffer the same problem as the story writing: Too serious to be fun to read, not serious enough to be compelling. I can't speak for the entire plot, but of the roughly seven hours I've played so far it's been serviceable, with some hiccups and questionable moments during cutscenes here and there. The story is fine, if a little boring, but certainly not remarkable. [ STYLE ] The art is very good, and aesthetically pleasing throughout. The music, not as much. The soundtrack used in this game isn't memorable or particularly even enjoyable to listen to most of the time -- it's just kind of there to fill in the background so it isn't dead air. But rather than fading out of mind, it pulls me out of the experience a little. Not much else to say here, the game would benefit from tighter direction of the music. [ CONCLUSION ] Right now, this is not a fun game. It is an okay game at best, and sometimes that's enough for the average player to squeeze enjoyment out of it. If this is you, don't let this review discourage you from at least trying it out yourself. Otherwise, I find that it fails to deliver quality on many fronts -- but not so much that it can't be redeemed. In my opinion, there IS a base of a good game here, somewhere. But it would take much reworking to transform this into something memorable. I can't say it's something I'm holding out hope for, but hey, anything can happen.

title: Katana ZERO
analysis_text: Rating: 8/10 This is an absolutely amazing game, and one that often gets overshadowed by more popular titles in the genre of kill-them-all-in-a-cool-way games. The mechanics are extremely fun, and the inclusion of a full-speed level "playback" in a game centered around slow-mo mechanics takes away the usual distinct lack of coolness that comes with slow-mo. However, I think what often gets glossed over in discussions of this game is the story. At its core, this is a fascinating story about PTSD and the military-industrial complex. At times, it can get a little too unncessarily edgy (by which I mean the edginess doesn't add to the story), but it piqued my interest overall. The only real criticism I can level at this game (besides the occasional edginess) is that it's too short. The mechanics and areas feel too brief to really sink my teeth into them, and far too much of the story is left up in the air. The developers have been working on a (free!) DLC, though, so here's hoping it will expand further on the interesting elements of the gameplay and plot!

title: Small Saga
analysis_text: This is a really good game and I'd recommend giving it a chance! The story is good, even if it is somewhat predictable. The characters were mostly likeable. The combat is turn-based with a simple yet fun action cost economy. You can somewhat customize your party with their own individual skill tree that you can change on the fly, and for free, to fit the situation you are in or just prefer. There are no random encounters in the traditional sense, all fights are set which, to me, gives off a DnD-esque feel. My only real criticism would be that I wanted the game to be longer, more side areas to explore, as the game felt short. Don't get me wrong, the game doesn't feel rushed but I just wanted more.

title: In Stars And Time
analysis_text: If there one characteristic I'm certain on, In Stars And Time's writing takes out many dialogue flourishes and facial expressions to make the characters WORK, especially across many, many, many, loops. Those interactions changing across the loops is how I see this story suits itself to a game. On the flipside, I not so sure I felt like gameplay should really take this long, owning to how combat is "required" with a certain fast traveling resource that feels somehow separate from the story, and yet is part of the story. I suppose that resource is just-- not gelling with the story in a game technical sense. I suppose, the story doesn't have much interactions with that resource outside of the resource being used to force the player to battle enemies? Except, enemies aren't *the* problem, rather it is the environment that acts as the challenge posed by the story. Enemies are just there, with very little interactions compared to the environment. With that said, I enjoyed In Stars And Times for bringing out these lovable dorks of main party, and an excellent showcase of dialogue tricks... Oh, I suppose I should say the game does a lot with very little in regards to maps & music. Classic pitch shifting, hahaha!

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: I'm sad to give this a negative review but as the game went on, it only got worse and worse until I couldn't take the game seriously anymore. The cast is entirely queer, including one person with neopronouns which is nice to see. The story and characters are generally very shallow, and around the midpoint of the game each chapter starts feeling monotonous as the plot takes too many twists and turns to have been planned out beforehand. Combat is generally enjoyable, though in the late game health pools start scaling up and it's hard not to want a defensive build when a couple bad timings could cost 3/4 of a party member's health bar. Assigning equipment is rather unwieldy, as there's too many choices that are hard to compare to each other and become obsolete every other chapter, as well as completely arbitrary weapon upgrades that are just a money sink. There's adequate accessibility options to both autocomplete action commands as well as fights themselves, and also an option to display content warnings which is very much appreciated. The ending solidified my negative review. No specifics, but [spoiler] after defeating what you'd think to be the final boss, another character unleashes barely-hinted at powers and you have to slog through a whole other multi-phase boss fight with them that I guess is supposed to be sad? the music in the fight is orchestral and somber but it's a full encounter that's only a little lower in difficulty compared to the previous boss. it's just baffling how the pace could be killed THAT quickly. [/spoiler] to its credit, the music is very good, though I think playing songs with lyrics during some boss fights was a mistake. it's undoubtedly the best part of the game, alongside the charming pixel art graphics. if you do play ikenfell, feel free to spin the control stick around in battle to fly into the sky!!

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: tl;dr -- The storytelling and the soundtrack are pretty good. The gameplay falls off quickly, starting from the mid-game. Early game is balanced well and enjoyable. Chapter boss HP scales exponentially and their damage scales linearly. Your damage from levels and your damage from gear scale VERY linearly. Which means your damage will get outpaced starting from the mid-game. Late game, the bosses start to hit you for 45-80% of your HP while you will hit them for 3-4% of their HP: If you build damage, you deal 4% and take 80-100% of your HP per boss hit. If you build tank, you deal 3% and take 30-45% per boss hit. Either way, the boss fight will take 60-90 minutes and will cycle through the same 3 mechanics. PRO TIP: enable "auto-victory" and click it often.

title: Ikenfell
analysis_text: This is a fine title if you're a really big fan of turn-based tactical combat, but the only 2 possible selling points - combat and story - leave some MAJOR holes. Combat- It's slow. Tedious and repetitive. Part of this is because of the "combat timing" interaction, where abilities have a slightly randomized pattern to make it harder to get perfect defense, but that really doesn't excuse it when increasing combat speed isn't an option. Some enemy attack animations (paper airplanes) can make a single instance of combat last for more than 15 seconds before you have the *option* to cheat for instant victory. Buffs and debuffs typically last 3 turns, and you're expected to use them a lot for any hard combat. Bosses almost always spawn adds to slow you down, have tons of health, and usually don't hurt. In some cases, they also have several dull phases. Further, characters can't aim sideways. There's no explanation given, but you're on a 3x12 or so board, and being next to a target is generally a problem. In the end, the combat isn't really difficult and doesn't require a lot of thinking. You keep up your buffs, debuffs, and wail on the enemy for as long as it takes to make combat end. Most items are prohibitively expensive to use outside of hard combat situations, and the only remedy for this status is copious amounts of stealing - which, again, extends each and every combat, and can only be done by 1 character. The story: Apart from major gaps in the story, minor characters steal the spotlight at the end for no apparent reason, few of the characters are actually likable, and there's a weird disconnect between how the avatars are presented in game and the apparent ages and actions of the characters themselves. The ending scenes don't even seem to relate to the events that occur during the game. The secrets in the game, after a ton of hunting, will lead you to secret bosses! These, like the others, generally aren't hard, but expect to take 20-45 minutes *each* to defeat. They will not offer additional story content or any fun lore/interactions. Negative ranting aside, the music in the game is genuinely incredible and worth listening to without playing the game itself. It might be the only reason I felt compelled to finish the game.
